The path is at (R(k),D(k)) after k moves, since R increases x by 1 and D increases y by 1. Thus the path visits cell (a,b) exactly when some k satisfies R(k)=a and D(k)=b. Because R(k)+D(k)=k, this can only happen at k=a+b, so visiting (a,b) is equivalent to the prefix of length a+b having exactly a R moves. Since the prefix length is a+b, having a R moves also means having (a+b)-a=b D moves. Conversely, if the prefix of length a+b has a R moves and b D moves, then after those a+b moves the path is at (a,b). Therefore forbidding a visit to (a,b) is exactly forbidding strings whose prefix of length a+b contains a R moves, equivalently whose count-prefix (a,b) occurs. Applying this to the five forbidden cells gives: (2,2) forbids prefix length 4 with 2 R; (4,3) forbids prefix length 7 with 4 R; (5,6) forbids prefix length 11 with 5 R; (7,5) forbids prefix length 12 with 7 R; (8,8) forbids prefix length 16 with 8 R. A valid string must avoid all five prefix-count conditions. These exclusions are independent of the no-RRR/no-DDD condition and of the checkpoint condition.

- Never take three R moves consecutively and never take three D moves consecutively.

- For lexicographic comparison use `D<R`.

Question: Give the number of valid paths and the lexicographically first valid move string.
